progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: bacteria are single cells with a wall containing peptidoglycan; pathogens and hosts; viruses are not cells. From b03: pathogens enter through breaks in the skin and through mucous membranes; fimbriae help bacteria grip against mucus. From b05 (playlist order, not a route prerequisite): a plant defends cell by cell because it has no circulating immune cells. From Year 11: cells, membranes, organelles including lysosomes (sacs of digestive enzymes); blood vessels and capillaries carry blood through tissues; enzymes. Not assumed: innate and adaptive immunity, mast cells, histamine, inflammation and its causes, neutrophils, macrophages, phagocytes and phagocytosis, dendritic cells, lymph and lymph nodes, T cells, fever as a deliberate response, pus.
progression.startsWith: Follow barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis. The video opens: In 1882, the zoologist Élie Metchnikoff pushed a rose thorn into a see-through starfish larva.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining how barriers keep most microbes out (skin's dead, flaking outer layers; mucus and cilia; stomach acid; lysozyme); defining the innate immune system (the barriers plus the fast responses after a breach); explaining how a breach triggers inflammation (damaged cells and mast cells release chemicals; histamine widens small vessels and makes them leaky, so fluid and blood proteins seep out) and linking redness, warmth, swelling and pain to those causes and to their purpose (delivering cells and proteins); explaining how neutrophils leave the blood and follow a chemical trail; describing phagocytosis step by step (bind, wrap, seal inside, lysosomes digest); explaining pus, and fever as a response when infection spreads; explaining how dendritic cells carry pieces of the pathogen to a lymph node and alert T cells, starting the adaptive response while the innate response is still going; comparing innate and adaptive responses and saying how they work together; interpreting a dye leak experiment and explaining the effects of a neutrophil adhesion defect.
progression.nextLesson: how B cells recognise and target an antigen (route entry bio-m7-b07).

teaching.task: A splinter pushes bacteria through your skin. What does your body do in the first hours, before any defence built for that pathogen is ready, and how do those first defences hold the bacteria back?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why animals can respond differently from plants (cells travel in blood; scene 2); how each barrier stops entry, not just its name (the 2025 Q21 marker comment; scene 3); why a splinter needs a second line (barrier broken; scene 4); what causes each sign (wider vessels, leaky walls, chemicals and pressure; scenes 5 and 6); why the signs help (delivery of cells and proteins; scene 6); how neutrophils find bacteria (stick, squeeze out, follow a trail that is strongest near the bacteria; scene 7); how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium without digesting itself (sealed bubble, then lysosomes; scene 8); why pus forms (scene 9); how the adaptive response is started (dendritic cells carry pieces to a lymph node; scene 10); why innate and adaptive are one interacting response, not two lists (the 2024 Q32 marker comment; scene 11). Visible case: the same splinter tissue changing in place from scene 4 to 9. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scene 3 (two plates, two chips) and scene 6 (the cause list) are the densest, so only the current row or chip is bright.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In 1882 Elie Metchnikoff pushed a rose thorn into a see-through starfish larva and by morning moving cells had crowded around it, with no antibodies involved, so the question is what the body does first when a splinter carries bacteria into the skin, before any defence built for that pathogen is ready. Animals, unlike the banksia, can send defending cells through the blood, but a pathogen first has to get in. Barriers come first: skin's dead, flaking outer layers, mucus and cilia in the airways, stomach acid and lysozyme. A splinter breaks that wall, and the innate immune system (defences you are born with, acting the same way against many pathogens) takes over. Damaged cells and mast cells raise the alarm, histamine widens and leaks the small vessels, and the four signs of inflammation are traced to their causes as a delivery route for cells and proteins rather than a failure. Signal chemicals strongest near the bacteria draw neutrophils to stick, squeeze out and crawl in, and neutrophils and macrophages act as phagocytes that bind, engulf and digest bacteria with lysosome enzymes; pus and fever are explained, and dendritic cells carry pieces of bacteria to a lymph node to start the slower, specific adaptive response. The two speeds work together, and the memory aid is block, alarm, eat, alert. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In 1882, the zoologist Élie Metchnikoff pushed a rose thorn into a see-through starfish larva. By the next morning, moving cells had crowded around the thorn. A starfish larva makes no antibodies, yet its cells found the intruder and closed in. Your body runs a similar response when a splinter carries bacteria into your skin. So what happens first, before any defence built for that pathogen is ready?
teaching.understandingCheck: 13a: explain a dye leak result from histamine, and how that change helps defence (analyse the chemical change and the physical change it causes). 13c: explain three observations in a child whose neutrophils can't stick to vessel walls (the route's stop: how innate cells reach and contain a pathogen). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ2-02: "analyse responses to the presence of pathogens by assessing the physical and chemical changes that occur in the host animals cells and tissues (ACSBL119, ACSBL120, ACSBL121, ACSBL122)". B7-IQ3-01: "investigate and model the innate and adaptive immune systems in the human body (ACSBL119)". Physical changes taught: vessels widening, walls becoming leaky, swelling, neutrophils leaving the blood, engulfing, pus. Chemical changes taught: alarm signals from damaged cells, histamine, signal chemicals that form a trail, digestive enzymes in lysosomes, temperature signals in fever. Verb "analyse" (identify components and the relationship between them): attempt 1 asks why one result follows from one chemical change, and scene 6 links each sign to its cause. "Investigate and model": the response strip and the aligned tissue plates are the model (route change 6); this video models the innate half and alerts the adaptive half, which b07 and b08 model.

design.visualSystem: One infection site board. Left two-thirds: painted tissue and cell plates on which each change is shown in place: a low-zoom cut section of skin with the splinter (an aligned pair, normal and inflamed) and a close-up of the tissue under the splinter tip (an aligned triplet: early, inflamed, contained), whose changes are revealed by masked regions of the next plate at the cue where each is narrated (the small vessel widens, fluid appears, the mast cell empties, a neutrophil squeezes out; the vessel is a small venule just past a capillary, and every on-screen tag calls it "small vessel", never "capillary"), as in b05's root cell pair. Phagocytosis is an aligned set of four macrophage plates (the existing "before" plate plus three new partners). Right third: the coded response strip, four rungs filled as taught, top to bottom: "always there: barriers" (scene 3), "minutes: inflammation" (scene 5), "hours: phagocytes" (scene 7), "days: adaptive" (scene 10, amber; the rung b07 and b08 expand). A bracket labelled "innate" spans the first three rungs from scene 4. The strip is the model the syllabus asks for, and its four rungs carry the memory aid (scene 12) and the decision rule (scene 14). No people, hands or faces: the body appears only as tissue sections, cells and one organ (a lymph node); the skin block is an isolated cut section with no limb or finger. The starfish larva in the hook is a whole animal, not a person. Coded elements are abstract only (no coded lymph node, cell or thermometer icons): the response strip, a vessel channel (two ink lines), chemical gradients as soft concentric rings, small coded specks for released chemicals and microbes in motion, arrows, a temperature set-point gauge (a short vertical scale with a moving mark, no thermometer icon), chips, glosses and step counters. Scale: the close-up spans about 0.15 mm; within it, bacteria (about 2 µm) are small rods, red blood cells about 7 µm, a neutrophil about 12 µm, a mast cell about 12 µm and a macrophage about 20 µm, and grey size tags say so where it matters (scene 8). Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
